title: Race to the Moon
summary: A president promised that Americans would walk on the Moon within ten years, even though nobody yet knew how. Robot probes crashed into the Moon, photographed its hidden side and landed on it, while astronauts practised meeting and joining spaceships in orbit. There were sad accidents too, but by Christmas 1968 three astronauts were circling the Moon and taking a famous photo of our blue Earth rising over it.

sections.heading: A Promise Nobody Knew How to Keep
paragraphs: In the spring of 1961 the young American president, John F. Kennedy, was having a bad few weeks. On 12 April Yuri Gagarin had orbited the Earth. A few days later, an American-backed invasion of Cuba at the Bay of Pigs had failed badly. Kennedy asked his vice-president, Lyndon Johnson, to find out whether there was any space goal where the United States had a real chance of beating the Soviet Union. The experts' answer was surprising: probably not a space station, and probably not orbiting more people, because the Soviets' powerful R-7 rocket gave them a head start. But a landing on the Moon was so hard that both countries would need brand-new giant rockets. In that race, the Americans might win.

On 25 May 1961 Kennedy stood in front of the United States Congress and asked for a huge amount of money. 'I believe that this nation should commit itself to achieving the goal, before this decade is out, of landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to the Earth,' he said. Remember that at that moment the only American who had been to space was Alan Shepard, for about 15 minutes. NASA did not have a rocket big enough, a spacecraft able to land on the Moon, a spacesuit for walking there, or even a plan for how to do it. Polls showed that many Americans thought it was a waste of money.

Kennedy made his case again on 12 September 1962, on a hot day in the football stadium of Rice University in Houston, Texas, near where NASA was building its new centre to control spaceflights. About 40,000 people listened. 'We choose to go to the Moon,' he said, and repeated it, explaining that the country would do it and other things 'not because they are easy, but because they are hard'. He described a rocket taller than a football field is long, built of metals not yet invented, that would have to survive heat about half that of the surface of the Sun on its way home. He even made a joke about the local college football rivalry, asking why Rice played Texas, a much bigger and stronger team.

The speech, written largely with his speechwriter Ted Sorensen, became one of the most famous ever given about science and exploration. Kennedy did not live to see the goal reached. He was assassinated in Dallas on 22 November 1963. Soon afterwards NASA's launch site in Florida was named the John F. Kennedy Space Center, and the country kept working towards his deadline as a kind of memorial.

sections.heading: Robots Go First
paragraphs: Before people could land on the Moon, someone had to answer some very basic questions. What did the surface look like close up? Were there safe flat places to land? And was the ground solid at all? Some scientists, most famously the astronomer Thomas Gold, worried that the Moon might be covered in deep, fluffy dust that would swallow a landing spaceship like quicksand. The only way to find out was to send robots.

The Soviet Union struck first again. In September 1959 its probe Luna 2 slammed into the Moon, becoming the first human-made object to reach another world. It was not a gentle arrival: the probe hit at more than 3 km per second, near the region called Mare Imbrium, the Sea of Showers. It carried small metal badges with the Soviet coat of arms, which were scattered on impact.

Just a month later, Luna 3 did something even more amazing. The Moon always keeps the same face turned towards Earth, so no human had ever seen its far side. Luna 3 swung around behind the Moon in October 1959 and took pictures on photographic film. Then, inside the probe, the film was developed, dried and scanned, and the images were sent back by radio, line by line, like a slow fax. The pictures were blurry and grainy, but they showed for the first time that the far side looks different: it has very few of the big dark plains, the lunar 'seas', that make the 'face' of the Man in the Moon.

The United States had a rough start. The first six of its Ranger probes, designed to photograph the Moon as they dived into it, all failed in one way or another. Then, in July 1964, Ranger 7 worked perfectly, sending back more than 4,000 sharp pictures in its last minutes before crashing. The final photos showed craters only about a metre wide.

The next big question, the dust, was answered on 3 February 1966, when the Soviet Luna 9 made the first soft landing on the Moon, in the Ocean of Storms. It was protected by inflatable airbags, bounced several times, and then opened four metal petals like a flower to stand upright. Its camera sent back the first pictures ever taken on the surface of another world, showing rocks and a horizon about 1.4 km away. Astronomers at the Jodrell Bank radio telescope in England picked up the signal, recognized that it used the same format newspapers used to send photos, and a British newspaper decoded and printed the pictures before the Soviets released them. Most importantly, Luna 9 had not sunk. The ground could hold a spacecraft.

Four months later, on 2 June 1966, the American Surveyor 1 made a soft landing too, using braking rockets and three legs, much as a crewed lander would. It sent back more than 10,000 pictures. Meanwhile, five American Lunar Orbiter probes, in 1966 and 1967, photographed almost the whole Moon from orbit so that NASA could pick safe, smooth landing sites for astronauts.

sections.heading: Gemini: Practice in Pairs
paragraphs: Getting to the Moon would need skills nobody had yet. How do you fly two spacecraft close together in orbit and join them? Can people live in a tiny cabin for a week or more, the time a Moon trip would take? Can an astronaut do useful work outside in a spacesuit? NASA needed a training programme, and it built one between Mercury and Apollo. Because its capsule carried two astronauts side by side, it was named Gemini, the Latin word for twins and the name of a constellation.

The reason meeting in orbit mattered so much was NASA's plan for the Moon, chosen in 1962 and pushed hard by a Langley engineer named John Houbolt. Instead of landing one enormous spaceship on the Moon, Apollo would send two craft joined together. A command ship would stay circling the Moon while a small, light lander took two astronauts down to the surface. Afterwards the top half of the lander would blast off and meet the command ship in lunar orbit. This idea, called lunar orbit rendezvous, saved so much weight that a single giant rocket could do the job. But it only worked if astronauts could reliably find and dock with another spacecraft, far from home. If it failed, the moonwalkers would be stranded. Gemini would test it.

The first crewed Gemini flight, Gemini 3, launched on 23 March 1965 with Gus Grissom and John Young. It lasted under five hours, but it did something no earlier American capsule could: the astronauts fired thrusters to change the shape and height of their orbit, actually steering their spacecraft from one path around the Earth to another. That skill would be essential for chasing another spacecraft. The flight is also remembered for a joke. Young had secretly carried a corned beef sandwich aboard and offered Grissom a bite. Crumbs floating around a cabin full of electronics could be dangerous, and some members of Congress were not amused, so later crews ate only approved space food: bite-sized cubes, freeze-dried meals that had to be mixed with water, and drinks squeezed from pouches.

Ten crewed Gemini flights launched in 1965 and 1966, each on a Titan II rocket, another former missile. In June 1965, on Gemini 4, Ed White made the first American spacewalk. He floated outside for over 20 minutes, pushing himself around with a small hand-held gas gun, and enjoyed it so much that he did not want to come back in, later calling it the saddest moment of his life. In August, Gemini 5 stayed up for about eight days, long enough for a round trip to the Moon.

Then came the most daring test. In December 1965 Frank Borman and Jim Lovell launched on Gemini 7 for a marathon: nearly 14 days crammed into a cabin about the size of the front seat of a small car. While they were up there, a second capsule, Gemini 6A with Wally Schirra and Tom Stafford, was meant to chase and meet them. Its first launch attempt, on 12 December, ended with a fright when the engines lit and then shut down after about one and a half seconds. The rocket stayed on the pad, and Schirra, judging correctly that it was not going to fall or explode, decided not to pull the ejection handle. Three days later, on 15 December, Gemini 6A flew perfectly.

Within about six hours Schirra had steered his capsule to Gemini 7. The two spacecraft flew together for hours, at times as close as about 30 centimetres, travelling around the Earth at about 28,000 km/h. The astronauts could see each other's faces through the windows. Schirra held up a sign for Gemini 7 to read, and before coming home the 6A crew surprised Mission Control by playing 'Jingle Bells' on a tiny harmonica and some bells they had smuggled aboard. Gemini had shown that a rendezvous in space was possible.

sections.heading: Armstrong's Wild Spin
paragraphs: Meeting another spacecraft was one thing; actually locking onto it was the next step. For this, NASA launched an uncrewed target rocket called an Agena, with a docking collar on its nose. On 16 March 1966, Gemini 8, flown by Neil Armstrong and David Scott, caught up with its Agena and gently slid its nose into the collar. It was the first time two spacecraft had ever docked in orbit.

About half an hour later, the joined spacecraft began to roll for no obvious reason. The astronauts undocked, thinking the Agena was the problem, but the spinning got much worse. One of Gemini's own small steering thrusters had become stuck on, probably because of an electrical fault, and was firing nonstop. Soon the capsule was whirling at nearly one full turn every second. Armstrong and Scott's vision began to blur, and there was a real danger they would black out.

Armstrong kept his head. He switched off the main steering thrusters and used a separate set meant for re-entry to slowly stop the spin. It worked, but using that fuel meant the mission rules required an immediate return. Gemini 8 came down in the western Pacific after only about 10 hours and 41 minutes, instead of the three days planned. NASA's managers noticed how calmly Armstrong had handled a life-threatening emergency, and that reputation would matter three years later.

The last flight, Gemini 12 in November 1966, solved the spacewalking problem. Earlier spacewalkers had become exhausted and overheated, because without something to brace against, every twist of a wrench spins your own body the other way. Buzz Aldrin had trained underwater, where floating is a little like weightlessness, and the spacecraft was given handholds and foot restraints. Taking regular rests, Aldrin worked outside for a total of about five and a half hours. By the end of Gemini, NASA knew how to rendezvous, dock, spend two weeks in space and work outside. Now it needed the Moon ship itself.

sections.heading: Fire on Pad 34
paragraphs: The first Apollo flight with a crew was planned for early 1967. Its astronauts were Gus Grissom, a veteran of Mercury and Gemini; Ed White, America's first spacewalker; and Roger Chaffee, a young Navy pilot preparing for his first flight. On 27 January 1967 they were strapped into their command module on top of an unfuelled Saturn IB rocket at Launch Complex 34 at Cape Kennedy, for what was called a 'plugs-out' test: a full rehearsal of the countdown with the spacecraft running on its own power. Because there was no fuel in the rocket, the test was not considered dangerous.

The cabin was filled with pure oxygen at slightly more than normal air pressure, as had been done in earlier spacecraft. In pure oxygen, things that normally burn slowly, such as nylon netting and Velcro patches, burn extremely fast. At about 6:31 in the evening, a spark, most likely from damaged wiring, started a fire. It spread through the cabin in seconds. The hatch was a heavy door that opened inwards and needed several steps to open, and the rising pressure of the hot gases held it shut. Ground crews rushed to help through smoke and heat, but within moments it was too late. All three astronauts died.

The whole country mourned, and some people asked whether the Moon goal should be abandoned. Instead, NASA and its contractors examined every part of the spacecraft. The command module was redesigned: a new hatch that could swing outwards in a few seconds, fireproof cloth for spacesuits, self-extinguishing materials, better-protected wiring, and a cabin atmosphere on the launch pad of 60 per cent oxygen and 40 per cent nitrogen instead of pure oxygen. Crewed Apollo flights were delayed by about 20 months. Many engineers later said the tragedy made the spacecraft far safer, and that Apollo might not have succeeded without those changes. The mission was renamed Apollo 1 in the crew's honour.

sections.heading: Trouble on the Other Side
paragraphs: The Soviet Union was racing too, but in secret, and it was having troubles of its own. On 14 January 1966 Sergei Korolev, the Chief Designer who had led Sputnik and Gagarin's flight, died during an operation, aged 59. Only after his death did the Soviet government reveal his name to the public. His team lost its strongest leader just as it faced its hardest job. Korolev's long rivalry with the top engine designer, Valentin Glushko, had also left his Moon rocket, the N1, with a difficult design: its first stage needed 30 engines firing together.

The Soviets also had a new spacecraft, Soyuz, meaning 'union'. On 23 April 1967 cosmonaut Vladimir Komarov launched on the first crewed Soyuz flight. Almost at once things went wrong: one of the two solar panels, which made electricity from sunlight, failed to unfold, leaving the ship short of power, and other systems began to fail. A second Soyuz, which was meant to launch the next day and meet him, was cancelled. Controllers brought Komarov home early. During the descent on 24 April, the main parachute did not come out and the reserve parachute tangled. The capsule hit the ground hard and Komarov was killed. He was the first person to die during a space mission. His backup for the flight had been Yuri Gagarin.

Soyuz flights stopped for about 18 months while the spacecraft was improved, and the design that came out of those fixes has flown, in updated versions, ever since. Meanwhile, the Soviets prepared a smaller project: a crew flight looping around the Moon without landing. In September 1968 an uncrewed version, Zond 5, flew around the Moon and back carrying two tortoises, along with fruit-fly eggs, plants and other tiny living things. The tortoises splashed down in the Indian Ocean and survived, becoming the first living things to travel around the Moon and come home. To American planners, it looked as if cosmonauts might be next.

sections.heading: Apollo 8: Christmas at the Moon
paragraphs: In October 1968 Apollo 7, with Wally Schirra, Donn Eisele and Walter Cunningham, tested the redesigned command module in Earth orbit for 11 days and sent the first live television broadcasts from an American spacecraft. It worked well. But the lunar module, the lander, was badly behind schedule. In the summer of 1968 a NASA manager named George Low suggested a bold idea: instead of waiting, send the next crew all the way to the Moon, to orbit it without a lander. The giant Saturn V had flown only twice, both times without people, and the second flight had had problems. Even so, NASA agreed. Some of the reasons were technical, and some were worry about what the Soviets might do next.

On 21 December 1968 Frank Borman, Jim Lovell and Bill Anders became the first people to ride a Saturn V. A few hours later, a burn of the third stage pushed them out of Earth orbit at about 39,000 km/h. They were the first humans ever to leave the neighbourhood of Earth, and the first to see the whole planet as a round ball hanging in space. The trip took about three days. On 24 December, as Apollo 8 swung behind the Moon, its radio signal was cut off by the Moon itself. Behind the Moon, the crew fired their engine to slow down and slip into orbit. If the burn had failed, they would have swung around and back towards Earth. Mission Control waited in nervous silence until, right on time, Lovell's voice came back. They were in lunar orbit.

For about 20 hours, Apollo 8 circled the Moon ten times, roughly 110 km above its grey, cratered surface. The astronauts were the first people to see the far side with their own eyes. They photographed possible landing sites. Then, on the fourth orbit, the spacecraft turned, and the crew suddenly saw the blue and white Earth rising above the Moon's horizon. Anders grabbed a camera loaded with colour film and took the picture now called 'Earthrise'. It showed our whole planet small and beautiful against black space, above a lifeless grey landscape. Many people say it changed how humans think about Earth, and it is often credited with helping to inspire the first Earth Day in 1970.

That night, Christmas Eve, the crew made a television broadcast from lunar orbit. Taking turns, they read the opening verses of the Book of Genesis from the Bible, about the creation of the heavens and the Earth. Borman ended by wishing a merry Christmas and God bless 'all of you on the good Earth'. It was one of the most-watched broadcasts in history up to that time. On Christmas Day the engine fired again behind the Moon to send them home, and when the signal returned, Lovell announced, 'Please be informed, there is a Santa Claus.' Apollo 8 splashed down in the Pacific Ocean on 27 December 1968, and the three astronauts were named Time magazine's Men of the Year.

sections.heading: The 400,000 People Behind the Astronauts
paragraphs: It is easy to think of the space race as a story about a few famous astronauts. In fact, at its peak, the Apollo programme involved roughly 400,000 people across the United States, along with more than 20,000 companies and universities. Only a small fraction worked for NASA directly. Most were employed by contractors: Boeing built the first stage of the Saturn V; North American Aviation built the second stage and the command module; Douglas built the third stage; Rocketdyne made the engines; and Grumman, on Long Island in New York, built the lunar module.

The work ranged from enormous to tiny. Welders joined fuel tanks big enough to hold swimming pools. At the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, engineers and programmers designed the guidance computer and its software. Factory workers, many of them women, wove the computer's permanent memory by hand, threading thin copper wires through or around tiny magnetic rings; each choice stored a one or a zero. Seamstresses at a company in Delaware stitched the moonwalkers' spacesuits from many layers of fabric, so precisely that a single badly placed stitch could mean a leak. Radio engineers ran giant dish antennas in California, Spain and Australia so that a spacecraft could always be heard as the Earth turned. Thousands of mathematicians, like Katherine Johnson, worked out trajectories.

The cost was enormous too. Apollo cost about 25 billion dollars at the time, roughly 257 billion dollars in 2020 money, and in the mid-1960s NASA received around 4 per cent of the whole US government budget. Many people argued, then and now, that the money should have been spent on problems on Earth. Supporters answered that the effort trained a generation of engineers and pushed forward computers, materials and electronics.

By early 1969, two more flights had tested the lunar module, first in Earth orbit and then in a full dress rehearsal near the Moon, coming within about 15 km of the surface. Everything was ready. In July 1969, at Launch Complex 39A in Florida, a white Saturn V rocket more than 110 m tall stood steaming in the summer heat, its tanks being filled with fuel, waiting for three astronauts and the most famous journey in history.

deepDive: How do you get to the Moon? In 1961 NASA argued over three plans. 'Direct ascent' meant building one colossal rocket, sometimes called Nova, to fly a whole spaceship to the Moon, land it tail-first, and fly it home. 'Earth orbit rendezvous', at first preferred by Wernher von Braun's team, meant launching two or more large rockets and assembling the Moon ship in Earth orbit. 'Lunar orbit rendezvous' (LOR), championed by John Houbolt of Langley, used one Saturn V and two spacecraft: only a small, light lander would go down to the surface, and only its upper half would come back up. Because every kilogram landed on the Moon must be carried there, slowed down and lifted off again, the savings snowballed. Houbolt wrote to NASA leaders that he felt like 'a voice in the wilderness', but by mid-1962 NASA chose LOR, and Gemini's rendezvous flights were designed to prove it. On the Soviet side, historians argue about why the USSR lost the Moon race even though it led early on. Reasons often given include: the government did not officially commit to a Moon landing until 1964, three years after Kennedy; money and effort were split between rival design bureaus led by Korolev, Vladimir Chelomei and others; Korolev and Glushko disagreed about engines, so the N1 was built around 30 smaller engines instead of a few giant ones; there was no big test stand to fire the whole first stage on the ground before flight; and Korolev's death in 1966 removed the leader who held everything together. Another debate concerns risk. Apollo 8 was a huge gamble: the Saturn V had flown only twice, and a failure of the engine behind the Moon could have stranded the crew. NASA leaders estimated the risks carefully, but they also felt time pressure from Kennedy's deadline and from Soviet Zond flights. Finally, the cost: in today's money Apollo is often estimated at around 250 billion dollars or more, and opinion polls through the 1960s showed many Americans did not think it was worth it, even though the Moon landings are now remembered as a national triumph.
funFact: According to the Smithsonian, the first musical instruments played in space were a tiny harmonica and a handful of small bells, used by the Gemini 6A crew to play 'Jingle Bells' in December 1965. Those instruments are now in the Smithsonian's collection.
